title: QuScope: An Open-Source Python Framework for Quantum-Circuit Simulation of Transmission Electron Microscopy
authors: Sean D. Lam, Roberto dos Reis
abstract: Image formation in transmission electron microscopy (TEM) is governed by the coherent evolution of the electron wavefunction through the specimen and the objective lens. This physics maps naturally onto the gate model of quantum computation. We present QuScope, an open-source Python framework that expresses the complete TEM image-formation pipeline as quantum circuits. The $N\times N$ electron wavefunction is amplitude-encoded in $2\log_2 N$ qubits, and every optical element, including phase-grating transmission, Fresnel propagation between specimen slices, and the aberrated objective lens, is implemented as a diagonal unitary conjugated by quantum Fourier transforms. On this foundation, QuScope v0.2.0 implements validated imaging pipelines, covering conventional TEM under the phase-object approximation, full multislice CTEM and STEM for thick specimens. All quantum results reported here come from exact, noise-free statevector simulation of the circuits on classical hardware, and every result is validated against a classical twin implementation. Quantum and classical multislice exit waves agree to unit fidelity, and all physical constants are verified against standard references. We provide transpiled quantum-resource estimates for each algorithm, an analysis of the diagonal-synthesis bottleneck that governs near-term hardware execution, and a fully tested, documented, and pip-installable package. QuScope v0.2.0 is available at https://github.com/QuScope/QuScope.
summary: This paper introduces QuScope, an open-source Python framework that models the entire process of Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) image formation using quantum circuits. It maps electron wavefunction propagation onto quantum gates, allowing simulations of techniques like CTEM and STEM. The work validates its accuracy by matching classical results to unit fidelity while also providing crucial resource estimates for future quantum hardware implementation.
main_problem: The core problem is simulating the complex, coherent evolution of an electron wavefunction through a specimen in Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM).
main_result: The authors developed QuScope, an open-source framework that successfully maps the entire TEM imaging pipeline onto quantum circuits, achieving unit fidelity with classical simulations.
method: The methodology involves amplitude encoding the $N 	imes N$ wavefunction into qubits and implementing physical operations (like Fresnel propagation or phase transmission) using diagonal unitaries conjugated by Quantum Fourier Transforms (QFTs).
model_or_system: The system is TEM, simulating electron wave propagation through specimens like $	ext{SrTiO}_3$. The physics maps to a quantum circuit model where optical elements are unitary gates.
key_observables: Image intensity ($|\psi_{	ext{image}}(\mathbf{r})|^2$), state fidelity ($\langle\psi_q|\psi_cangle|^2$), and resource estimates (gate counts, depth).
important_parameters: Grid size ($N 	imes N$), scattering strength ($\sigma V$), and error rates for noise analysis.
main_assumptions: The framework relies on the assumption that quantum simulation can accurately model wave propagation; limitations include the exponential cost of synthesizing arbitrary diagonal unitaries and decoherence effects in deep circuits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate transfer characteristics, probe intensity channeling through crystalline materials ($	ext{SrTiO}_3$), and comparisons between quantum and classical multislice results.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem mapping to quantum circuits, details the implementation of core components (QFTs, diagonal unitaries), validates the framework against classical simulations across various TEM techniques (CTEM, STEM), and concludes with resource estimation for near-term hardware.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, physics-driven application demonstrating how complex wave phenomena can be formulated as quantum circuits, offering valuable benchmarks for quantum simulation algorithms beyond standard chemistry or materials Hamiltonians.
